problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}-9y={x}^{2}.
$$

The corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{3x}$ and ${y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-3x}.$ 

According to the method of variation of parameters, we should seek a particular solution 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}
$$

that satisfies the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}={x}^{2} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that ${u}_{1}(x)=\int g(x)\,\text{d}x,$ find the function $g.$
worked_solution:
We notice that the forcing term is $f(x)={x}^{2}.$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{3x},\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-3x}.
$$

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions are independent by computing the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =({e}^{3x})({e}^{-3x})^{′}-({e}^{3x})^{′}({e}^{-3x}) \\  & =({e}^{3x})(-3{e}^{-3x})-(3{e}^{3x})({e}^{-3x}) \\  & =-3-3 \\  & =-6\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are linearly independent. 

Now, we have the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{({e}^{3x})}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{({e}^{-3x})}^{′}={x}^{2} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-3x}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}3{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}-3{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-3x}={x}^{2} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-3x}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to find an integral expression for ${u}_{1}.$ We start by eliminating ${u}_{2}^{′}$ from the second equation:

$$
{u}_{2}^{′}=-\frac{{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}}{{e}^{-3x}}=-{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{6x}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}-3{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-3x} & ={x}^{2} \\ 3{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}-3(-{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{6x}){e}^{-3x} & ={x}^{2} \\ 3{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x} & ={x}^{2} \\ 6{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x} & ={x}^{2} \\ {u}_{1}^{′} & =\frac{1}{6}{x}^{2}{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}_{1}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{6}{x}^{2}{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\ {u}_{1} & =\int \frac{1}{6}{x}^{2}{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\ {u}_{1} & =\int \frac{1}{6}{x}^{2}{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $g(x)=\frac{1}{6}{x}^{2}{e}^{-3x}.$
